pages.x: Iraq came out of its war with Iran owing tens of billions of dollars, much of it to Kuwait, its small, rich neighbour. Saddam Hussein accused Kuwait of pumping too much oil, which kept prices low, and of stealing Iraqi oil by drilling at a slant under the border. He also said Kuwait was rightly part of Iraq.

Before dawn on 2 August 1990 Iraqi tanks crossed the border, and within two days Iraq held all of Kuwait. The emir escaped to Saudi Arabia. Saddam declared Kuwait the nineteenth province of Iraq, his soldiers looted it, and his army now stood on the border of Saudi Arabia, which held a quarter of the world's oil.

President George H. W. Bush declared that the invasion would not stand. The United Nations put Iraq under sanctions and gave it until 15 January 1991 to leave. The United States built a coalition of dozens of countries, among them Arab states such as Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria, and over half a million American troops gathered in the Saudi desert.

On 17 January 1991 the coalition began to bomb Iraq, and for the first time the world watched a war live on television, as tracer fire lit up the night sky over Baghdad. Guided bombs and cruise missiles smashed air defences, bridges and power stations. Iraq fired Scud missiles at Israel, hoping to draw it in and split the coalition, but Israel held back.

On 24 February the ground war began. While Iraq waited for an attack from the sea and straight into Kuwait, the main coalition armies swung far out into the desert and hooked round behind them. Iraqi soldiers surrendered in their tens of thousands. After a hundred hours Bush called a halt, and Kuwait was free.

As they retreated, Iraqi troops set fire to Kuwait's oil wells. The smoke turned day into night, and fire-fighting teams from around the world took until November to put the last one out. Millions of barrels of oil were also poured into the Gulf, coating beaches and killing seabirds.

The coalition stopped short of Baghdad. Bush urged Iraqis to rise up, and Shia Arabs in the south and Kurds in the north did, but Saddam's helicopters and tanks crushed them, and over a million Kurds fled into the mountains. Iraq lived under UN sanctions for the next twelve years.

The Gulf War showed the power of America's new weapons, and seemed to promise a world where nations would stand together against aggression. But Saddam stayed in power, and American troops stayed in Saudi Arabia, which enraged Osama bin Laden. The war's unfinished business led to the Iraq War of 2003.
pts: The ground war lasted a hundred hours
Kuwait's oil wells burned for months
